boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Parsdorf entry (12 October 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: Wrede's Bavarian advanced guard of Bernadotte's 1st corps, with French cavalry support, pursuing Kienmayer's rearguard from Munich to Parsdorf. The captures of 13 October, which Krauss places at Parsdorf on that day, and the cavalry pursuit to the Inn are recorded only as a dating question (claim date-of-captures) and are not counted as this entry's figures. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart's entry gives no strength for either side.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription: it names the sides and commanders and gives side B's loss, with no strength for either side. The strengths below come from the other sources. English rendering (ours): 'victory of the Bavarians under GM Wrede over the Austrians under FML Baron von Kienmayer'.

claims.value: Side A (Bavarian): the Bavarian corps' journal, in paragraphs it does not date (claim date-of-captures), says that Wrede put himself at the head of the 1st dragoons and the three remaining squadrons of the 3rd chevau-légers, 'the whole numbering only 240 horses', after sending Major Elbracht with a squadron toward Rosenheim and Wasserburg. When the Deutschmeister battalion surrendered he had only 42 files with him, having detached cavalry to both sides of the road to cover his flanks.
claims.rationale: Side A's own figures for the pursuing cavalry, read from the page images; the journal gives no figure for the rest of the Bavarian corps. '240 chevaux' counts horses (mounted men) at the start of the pursuit and '42 files' the files left at the surrender; the second is not converted into men. Wrede formed this group himself for the pursuit (claim side-a-command). English renderings (ours): 'ordered Major Elbracht of the 3rd chevau-légers to go with a squadron on the roads to Rosenheim and Wasserburg and put himself at the head of the 1st dragoons, which had just arrived, and of the three remaining squadrons of the 3rd chevau-légers, the whole numbering only 240 horses'; 'when this happened, the lieutenant general had only 42 files with him, because he had been forced, by the haste with which the enemy rearguard had to be reached, to detach a number of cavalry to the left and right of the road to secure the flanks'.

claims.rationale: French figures, read from the page images; Kellermann's support is given without a headcount, and no passage read says whether it came into action. Bernadotte's 80 chevau-légers and the journal's 42 files (claim side-a-pursuit-force) describe the same surrender and are kept apart. Who ordered Kellermann's support is not stated. claims.value: Bernadotte, marching from Ingolstadt on Munich, had placed the Bavarian corps at the head of his advance. By the Bavarian journal, Wrede could have forced Munich but preferred to give the enemy a golden bridge to spare the town; finding it evacuated, he ordered all his cavalry to follow at the trot and went ahead at the gallop with a squadron, then, judging the Austrian army to be in panic, pursued its rearguard at full speed with 240 horses and himself attacked the Deutschmeister battalion. Separately, Ameil and Bonnemain's French horsemen had turned the town and cut off the extreme rearguard.
claims.rationale: Decisions as the Bavarian corps' journal (printed by the French official history) and Alombert and Colin's narrative give them; Alombert and Colin add that the golden-bridge phrase is Wrede's own ('dit-il lui-même'). The journal is Wrede's side's account. English renderings (ours): 'marching from Ingolstadt on Munich, Bernadotte had placed the Bavarian corps at the advanced guard'; 'to spare the town of Munich the horrors of a fight, he preferred, he says himself, to make a golden bridge for the enemy'; 'he preferred to make a golden bridge for the enemy'; 'the lieutenant general ordered all his cavalry to follow him at the trot, going ahead himself at the gallop with a squadron of the 3rd chevau-légers'; 'chevau-légers, the whole numbering only 240 horses; reckoning on the panic terror that had seized the Austrian army, he pursued the enemy rearguard at full speed'; 'a little short of Parsdorf, the lieutenant general attacked'; Ameil and Bonnemain as in claim side-a-support.

claims.value: Krauss says FML Kienmayer had evacuated Munich in the night of 11-12 October before Bernadotte's advancing troops and fallen back on the 12th to Ampfing, continuing his retreat to the Inn. Bernadotte wrote that the Austrians began their retreat the evening before and continued it all night. No passage read names the commander of the rearguard caught near Parsdorf.

English renderings (ours): 'east of the Lech, FML Kienmayer had evacuated Munich in the night of 11 to 12 October before the advancing troops of Bernadotte and had fallen back on the 12th to Ampfing, from where he continued the retreat to the Inn' (the OCR reads 'Iini' for 'Inn'); 'they began their retreat yesterday evening and continued it all night'.

claims.value: Krauss dates to 13 October the capture by Bernadotte's advanced guard, at Parsdorf east of Munich, of an artillery park of 17 heavy guns and over 1,000 prisoners. The Bavarian journal records under 21 vendémiaire (13 October) the capture by Major Elbracht and Lieutenant Speeg of an artillery train of four howitzers, nine cannon and four mortars with its escort, a recruiting chest and 700 muskets, without naming the place. Its paragraphs on the entry into Munich and the pursuit, in which Wrede's horsemen took 1,100 prisoners from the rearguard and attacked the Deutschmeister battalion a little short of Parsdorf, follow that entry in print and are headed by subject, not by date. Bernadotte, writing to the Emperor from Munich on 20 vendémiaire (12 October) at 11.30 in the evening, reports that his advanced guard has pushed the enemy five leagues beyond Munich on the road to Hohenlinden, so the pursuit falls on the 12th (our reading). Alombert and Colin give the prizes of the 1st corps and the Bavarians, including the pursuit to the Inn on the 13th, as 19 guns, 150 horses, wagons and 1,500 prisoners.
claims.rationale: Bodart dates Parsdorf 12 October; Krauss places a capture at Parsdorf on the 13th. The journal's subject-headed paragraphs carry no date of their own; Bernadotte's letter of the 12th is the dated source for the pursuit. The journal's 4 + 9 + 4 pieces make 17 (our sum), Krauss's figure, so the two may describe the same convoy, but no passage read says so. Not resolved; the 13 October captures are not counted in this entry's figures (boundary note). English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'east of the Lech, Bernadotte's advanced guard had succeeded on the 13th, at Parsdorf, east of Munich, in seizing an artillery park of 17 heavy guns and taking over 1000 prisoners'; '21 vendémiaire (13 October). The position of the advanced guard was carried half a league forward'; 'capture of an artillery convoy. The same day Major Elbracht and Lieutenant Speeg, acting together, took an artillery train of four howitzers, nine cannon and four mortars, with the escort commanded by two officers, besides a recruiting chest and 700 muskets'; 'entry into Munich. The lieutenant general accordingly ordered all his cavalry to follow him at the trot'; 'he pursued the enemy rearguard at full speed, made 1100 prisoners on it'; 'capture of an enemy battalion of the Deutschmeister regiment. A little short of Parsdorf, the lieutenant general attacked'; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the Emperor. Munich, 20 vendémiaire year XIV (12 October 1805), at 11.30 in the evening'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Majesty that my advanced guard has pushed the enemy five leagues beyond Munich, on the road to Hohenlinden'; 'his cavalry pursues the Austrians as far as'; 'the total of the prizes made by the 1st corps and the Bavarians comes to 19 guns, 150 horses, wagons and 1500 prisoners'.

Wrede's advance went through Munich, with an aim to seize the heights of the Gasteig suburb beyond the Isar, and along the road to Hohenlinden; Bernadotte says his advanced guard pushed the enemy five leagues beyond Munich. The enemy's rearguard was caught a little short of Parsdorf, and its army stood in line behind Parsdorf on the height of Anzing.

claims.value: Side A's pursuit was made by cavalry alone, at the trot and gallop; on the great square of Munich Wrede found the burgomaster and a vast crowd gathered for the Elector's feast day and had to stop to drink the sovereign's health, and refreshments arrived for the troops. The journal notes that the enemy had put no obstacle at the 'passage du poste'. Side B had begun its retreat the evening before and continued it all night, some troops by the Wasserburg road and most by the Hohenlinden road.
claims.rationale: Movement as the journal, Bernadotte and Alombert and Colin report it; no supply return was inspected. English renderings (ours): 'he then took the trot with his cavalry and launched himself in pursuit of the Austrians'; 'he found there the burgomaster and a countless people gathered to celebrate the Elector's feast and the return of his troops. He had to stop his course to drink the health of the' [sovereign]; 'refreshments arrived for the troops'; 'the enemy having neglected to put the least obstacle at the crossing of the post'; 'some troops retired by the Wasserburg road, but the greater part took the Hohenlinden road'.

claims.value: Side A attacked: Wrede's cavalry pursued the Austrian rearguard from Munich and attacked a battalion of Deutschmeister short of Parsdorf, which surrendered; Bernadotte says the Bavarians fell alone on the enemy's rearguard. Side B was retreating.
claims.rationale: Pursuit counts as attacking. The journal shows Wrede deciding the pursuit himself on finding Munich evacuated (claim side-a-command); no order from above for it was found, so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings as in claims side-a-command and side-a-support.

open_questions: Deferred: the return of the Austrian troops at Munich that Bernadotte sent the Emperor (not found in the passages read); Krauss's text before p. 449 on Kienmayer's corps; any Bavarian account other than the corps journal printed by Alombert and Colin. The 'Beaux traits individuels' paragraph of the journal (OCR, p. 662) carries a figure seen only in the OCR and is not recorded.

Most consequential gap: side B's own account of the rearguard action and its strength. No Austrian report for 12 October was read; Krauss's 20,000 is Kienmayer's whole corps. An Austrian or Bavarian account of the pursuit could close it; none was identified in this pass.

Disputes kept as separate claims: the date of the captures at Parsdorf (Bodart 12 October, Krauss 13 October for the 17-gun park, the journal dating the convoy to the 13th and printing its undated paragraphs on the pursuit after that entry, while Bernadotte reports the pursuit on the 12th); side B's loss on the 12th (journal and Alombert and Colin 1,100, Bernadotte 600-700 and 1,100-1,200, Bodart about 1,600 with 9 guns); the surrender of the Deutschmeister battalion before 42 files (journal) or 80 chevau-légers (Bernadotte).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked); Alombert and Colin, t. III (the French official history, printing the Bavarian corps' journal, an interested account of Wrede's own side, and Bernadotte's letter of 12 October); Krauss (an Austrian history from the Kriegsarchiv files; his French movements depend on Alombert and Colin, and his Parsdorf sentence cites no source in the passage read).
